name: Cybersecurity Beyond Phishing
title: Cybersecurity Beyond Phishing
answer: Cybersecurity beyond phishing means protecting schools from attacks such as ransomware that can close schools for days and expose student data. It covers basic defenses, vendor contracts, and review of AI tools before they connect to district systems. It matters because a single breach can affect many districts and because staff use of AI can create new ways for sensitive information to leak.

sections.body: The idea is that school cybersecurity cannot stop at teaching people to spot phishing messages. Schools face ongoing attacks, including ransomware that holds systems hostage until payment, and such an attack can halt school for days and reveal student information. Basic safeguards, such as strong passwords with a second verification step, backups stored away from the main network, and timely software updates, reduce the risk. The problem also extends to vendors that hold student data, because a breach at one company can expose records from many districts at once. AI tools add another layer, since staff might paste sensitive details into general chat tools or link tools to district systems without review.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the text describes district-wide steps rather than separate steps by grade band. Schools should use strong passwords with a second verification step, keep regular backups separate from the main network, and apply software updates promptly. Contracts with vendors should require data protection, fast breach reporting, and cooperation with investigations. Districts should maintain a list of every vendor that holds student data and review that list on a regular schedule. For AI, staff should use the approved tool list from Chapter 3, and IT and privacy staff should review any tool before it connects to district data.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not present a study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It states that basic protections make a large difference, but that claim is offered as practical guidance rather than research. This idea therefore rests on practice and operational judgment rather than on research evidence described in the supplied text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that vendors remain part of the security picture and a breach at a vendor can expose data from many districts at once. AI tools create new security questions when staff paste sensitive information into general chat tools or connect tools to district systems without review. The decisions that stay with people include writing contract requirements for vendors, keeping and reviewing the vendor list, approving tools, and having IT and privacy staff review any tool before it connects to district data. The text does not say that any tool or vendor can be trusted automatically. It also does not treat the approved tool list as only a privacy measure, since it is a security measure as well.
